claims.text: The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles are sub-5 nm and have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibit a single-phase FCC structure.
The proposed heating protocol ramps the nanoparticles from ambient temperature to 800 °C in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm have a surface-to-volume ratio greater than 50%.
Above a critical temperature, surface-energy gradients override sluggish diffusion and drive Au and Cu segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu are lower-surface-energy constituents of AuCoCuNiPt and therefore preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu surface segregation creates a core-shell composition profile and lowers the activation energy for atomic migration.
The segregation-induced chemical-potential gradient enhances atomic mobility contrary to the sluggish-diffusion paradigm.
Surface free energy in sub-10 nm particles can override entropic stabilization of the bulk FCC phase.
Surface-energy-driven segregation leads to Ostwald ripening.
Heating drives a transition from elliptical or icosahedral particles to spherical particles by minimizing surface area.
Surface-enriched Au and Cu subsequently evaporate, contributing to particle disappearance.
Heating causes progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Elemental mapping will show Au and Cu surface enrichment before the affected particles disappear.
The critical onset occurs when the surface-energy contribution γA dominates the entropic contribution TΔS_mix.
The proposed mechanism applies strictly to nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
In particles larger than 50 nm, entropic stabilization and sluggish diffusion dominate and prevent rapid segregation and evaporation.
The silicon nitride substrate may influence surface-diffusion kinetics.
A truncated-octahedral nanoparticle has higher surface energy and should segregate or evaporate faster than an icosahedral nanoparticle at the same temperature.
